meta.title: Vahiny Mianatra Malagasy — Expanded Thematic Vocabulary
meta.description: Large thematic vocabulary dataset for a beginner English speaker (elderly learner). Official Malagasy is primary; Tsimihety (as spoken in Mandritsara) variants are marked where Bako's lessons give them. Sources: Peace Corps Malagasy Language Lessons (public domain), bako.blog thematic lessons (used as reference for this original compilation), malagasyword.org dictionary checks.
meta.audience: Elderly American beginner learner (absolute beginner, English speaker)

fields.id: stable slug, unique within the theme
fields.note: usage or culture note for the learner (optional)

conventions.tense_note: Verbs appear in the present (m-) form. Past = n-, future = h-: mihinana -> nihinana -> hihinana. Only the first letter changes.
conventions.audio_note: peace_corps_audio lists matching MP3s in MALAGASY ASSETS/Malagasy-Sakalava/ for listening practice.
conventions.bako_note: bako_lessons references the lesson PDFs in MALAGASY ASSETS/bako-blog-lessons/ (link out; get permission before republishing her PDFs).

words.note: All-purpose greeting, any time of day.
The most common greeting in Mandritsara; tompoko covers both sir and ma'am.
Official form; more politely: 'Manao ahoana tompoko?'
Bako's everyday form in Mandritsara. To several people: 'Manakory ianareo?'
Short for 'Mahasalama ve ianao?' — literally 'health?'
Standard reply to any 'how are you?'. Fa = but.
Classic follow-up after 'how are you?'
Polite modest reply — even when plenty has happened!
Said by an arriving guest, like a knock.
Host to guest. Also a vendor's 'come and buy', or inviting a passer-by to join a meal (they may answer 'Misaotra, mazotoa' = thanks, enjoy yours).
To one person; to several: 'Mipetraha!'
Warmer than plain misaotra.

words.en: Not at all / don't mention it.
words.note: Standard reply when thanked.
The most useful politeness word: squeezing past, small mistakes, softening requests.

words.en: Excuse me (passing) — may I get by?
words.note: Standard courtesy when squeezing past, e.g. on a taxi-brousse.
The Peace Corps lesson lists it as an equal of azafady.
The word used in the Bible — not for trivial slips.

words.en: No problem / it's OK / you're welcome
words.note: Standard reply to azafady and to thanks.
Place after any greeting or name: 'Salama tompoko!'

words.en: madam, Mrs (respectful for a married or older woman)

'Salama rahalahy!'
Lit. 'arrived well'. Said by the host, not by the arriving guest.
Said by the one leaving. Those staying reply 'Soava dia!' or 'Soa am-bifilana!'

words.en: Enjoy! / have a good day! / keep it up! / bye!
words.note: Bako: 'a versatile word like azafady'. Said before someone goes off to eat, rest, or work.
Official alternative: 'Mazotoa mihinana.' Reply: 'Misaotra ianao koa.'

words.en: Have a safe journey! / bon voyage!
words.note: soa (good) + va + dia (journey).
Lit. 'good at the returning' — wishing a safe return too.

words.en: See you later! (same day or next)
words.note: Lit. 'until we meet.'

words.en: See you in a bit! (minutes to hours, same day)

In reply to 'Misy ... ve?': 'Ia, misy' = yes, there is/are.
Goes at the sentence end: 'Amerikana ve ianao?' = Are you American?
Alternative to ve for yes/no questions.
Core request pattern (Peace Corps Lesson 8). Mba softens it further.
Very polite request — ideal phrasing for an elderly learner.
The most useful way to ask for anything.
Reply: 'Azo!' = got it / yes, you may.
Intensified apology; betsaka = very much, many.
Handy at the market and when being served food.
'Tsara ny andro' = the weather is nice. 'Tsara be!' = very good!
'Mora ve?' = is it cheap? Opposites: sarotra (hard), lafo (expensive).
Mahalala = to know someone. Reply: 'Faly mahalala anao koa!'
Between guest and host, especially in the highlands: alternating short formal greetings before real conversation.
Imperative of miandry (to wait).

words.en: Let's go! / come on! / go ahead!
words.note: 'Ndao handeha!' = let's go. Also said to let someone pass.
A very common exclamation.

themes.title: People & Family — Olona sy Fianakaviana

words.note: One word covers man, boy, and male.
One word covers woman, girl, and female.
Formal word: ray. Possessive attaches directly: dadako = my dad.
Formal word: reny. neniko = my mom.
Used in compounds: ray aman-dreny = parents.
'Aman-' links paired nouns: father-and-mother. My parents: 'ray aman-dreniko'.
vadiko = my spouse, vadinao = your spouse, vadiny = his/her spouse.

words.en: child, children (in relation to their parents)
words.note: 'Manana zanaka aho' = I have children. zanako = my child.
Not tied to the parent-relationship; also affectionate for adults.
tokana = only/single.
'Manana zoky firy ianao?' = How many older siblings do you have?

words.en: brother (said by a man; respectful 'brother' for any man)
words.note: A man says rahalahy for his brother; a woman says anadahy.
A woman says rahavavy for her sister; a man says anabavy.
dada + be = 'big father'. Also used respectfully for any elderly man.
neny + be = 'big mother'. Also respectful for any elderly woman.

words.en: uncle (father's side; respectful for any older man)
words.note: dada + toa. Malagasy consider uncles like parents.

words.en: aunt (mother's side; respectful for any older woman)

words.note: Official construction from Bako theme 1; Tsimihety uses special borrowed terms (e.g. 'Zama').
Nephews and nieces are treated like one's own children (Bako theme 1).
Informal modern loanword.
Family identity runs deep through ancestors in Malagasy culture.
The project name 'Vahiny Mianatra Malagasy' = 'A guest learning Malagasy'. Guests are honored: 'Tongasoa!'
Neutral, friendly word — an American learner will hear it often, always kindly.
'Manambady aho' = I'm married (present); nanambady (past); hambady (future).
'Mbola tsy mananjanaka izahay' = We don't have children yet.
'Manana zanaka telo aho' = I have three children. Negative: 'Tsy manana...'

words.en: to be married (lit. 'to have a spouse')
words.note: manana + vady contracts to manam-bady.
Counting children: 'Mananjanaka telo zahay: lahy iray, vavy roa.' = We have three children: one boy, two girls.
'Mpianatra teny malagasy aho' = I'm learning Malagasy.
'Mpampianatra anglisy' = English teacher.
Common self-description of most Malagasy.
Peace Corps Lesson 3: 'Mpiofana aho.'
Peace Corps Lesson 4 word.

culture_notes: Family terms shift with the speaker's gender: rahalahy/anadahy (brother) and rahavavy/anabavy (sister) swap depending on who is talking, and uncle/aunt terms differ by maternal vs paternal side.
Malagasy consider uncles and aunties like parents, cousins like siblings, and nephews/nieces like one's own children (Bako theme 1).
Possessives are suffixes on the noun (curriculum Week 7): -ko (my), -nao (your), -ny (his/her): vadiko, vadinao, vadiny, tranoko, zanany.

themes.title: Food & Drink — Sakafo sy Zava-pisotro

'Mofo gasy' = Malagasy rice-flour bread, sold warm at street stalls in the morning.
hena + kisoa = pig-meat.

Market order: 'atody telo' = three eggs (number after the noun).
Made into sweet 'koba' and brittle candies.
Classic road-trip snack, sliced thin and fried.
Loanword from French 'légume'.
The everyday green of rural Madagascar — edible boiled leaves of many plants.
'Tomaty' is also common.
Classic protein laoka. Green beans = tsaramaso tanora (young beans).
The tender shoots and leaves are also cooked as greens.
sira + mamy = salt + sweet.
Served with everything and VERY hot.
Lit. 'Malagasy onion'.
Lit. 'Egyptian onion' / 'big onion'.
Lit. 'leaf onion' / 'green onion'.
voa (fruit) + kazo (tree). Fruit is seasonal — except bananas.
The only fruit available year-round.
Also 'voasary be' = big orange.
Abundant Nov–Jan. Homophone trap: manga also means blue — context decides!
Madagascar's famous export lychee — the Christmas-season fruit.
Prized native pepper from forest vines.
Visitor's phrase: 'Mila rano amin'ny tavoahangy aho' = I'd like bottled water.
Made by boiling water in the rice pot after the rice is cooked; the national everyday drink.
Strong, sweet, served in small glasses — offered to every guest.
THB (Three Horses Beer) is the national brand.
Ceremonial staple — included for completeness, not a recommendation.
Present mihinana, past nihinana, future hihinana. Everyday alternative: misakafo.
misakafo maraina = have breakfast; atoandro = lunch; hariva = dinner.
'Misotro rano aho.' = I drink water.
'Matsiro be!' = very delicious! The compliment every host hopes for.
Gracious reply to more food: 'Voky misaotra!'
Peace Corps Lesson 6 pattern: te + h-verb = want to ...
'Mahandro vary aho.' Past nanandro, future hahandro.
'Ao an-dakozia' = in the kitchen (Bako theme 4 title).
sotro + be = big spoon.
Loanword; in villages people usually eat with a spoon or the right hand.
'Kaopy telo' = three cups — also the standard rice measure at market.
'Rano amin'ny tavoahangy' = bottled water.
Used for washing dishes and clothes.
Usually a charcoal stove.
'Tondroy ny latabatra' = point to the table — the TPR drill from Bako's kitchen lesson.
Traditional palm-leaf mat used for seating and sleeping.
THE market question. 'Ohatrinona ny vary?'
Polite market banter: 'Lafo be io! Mora azafady!'

words.en: Is it cheap? / can you lower the price?

words.note: Needed at small stalls.
'Mividy mofo izy.' = She is buying bread. Buyer = mpividy.
'Mivarotra vary izy.' = She sells rice. Past nivarotra; seller = mpivarotra.

words.en: to go shopping, go to market

words.note: 'Vary telo kapoaka' = three cups of rice — noun, then number, then measure.
'Voatabia telo toko' = three piles of tomatoes.
'Miantsena aho' = I'm going to market.
'Tsy mihinana trondro manta aho.' = I don't eat raw fish.

culture_notes: A Malagasy meal without rice is not a meal: someone who ate only bread will say 'Tsy nisakafo aho' (I haven't eaten).
The hostess pours water over your hands from a jug for washing before you eat — hold your hands over the basin.
'Mandrosoa' (come join us!) at mealtime is mandatory politeness; replying 'Misaotra, mazotoa' (thanks, enjoy yours) declines gracefully.

themes.title: Numbers & Money — Isa sy Vola

words.note: Lit. 'one on top of ten'.
Tens: digit + folo.
Hundreds: digit + jato.
So: dimy arivo = 5,000; fito arivo = 7,000.
SAME spelling as alina (night)! Context tells them apart. Roa alina = 20,000; enina alina = 60,000.
Efatra hetsy = 400,000; valo hetsy = 800,000.
tapitra (ended) + isa (number) — 'a number with an end'.
'Manana zoky firy ianao?' = How many older siblings do you have?
Lit. 'how many years are you?'
'Dimy ambin'ny enimpolo taona aho.' = I'm 65 (lit. five on top of sixty).
Lit. 'silver' — from the old silver-coin era.
1 ariary = 5 iraimbilanja. Prices are written in ariary (Ar).
Old unit; many people still compute mentally in francs — a quoted price may sound five times too big.
'Tsy misy madinika' = no change available.
'Misaotra betsaka' = thanks a lot.

construction_rules: Numbers are READ RIGHT TO LEFT: for 37 say the units digit first — 'fito ambin'ny telopolo' (seven on top of thirty).

'Ambin'ny' (short for 'ambony ny' = on top of) connects a units digit to tens/hundreds through 199. Examples: 11 = iraika ambin'ny folo; 37 = fito ambin'ny telopolo; 65 = dimy ambin'ny enimpolo; 183 = telo ambin'ny valonjato ambin'ny zato.
From 200 upward, 'sy' (and) replaces 'ambin'ny' for the final units: 205 = roanjato sy dimy; 221 = roanjato roapolo sy iray.

Tens = digit + folo (roapolo 20, sivifolo 90). Hundreds = digit + jato (telonjato 300). Thousands = digit + arivo (dimy arivo 5,000). Ten-thousands = digit + alina (roa alina 20,000). Hundred-thousands = digit + hetsy (valo hetsy 800,000).
Counting things, the noun comes FIRST and the number after: 'atody telo' = three eggs; 'vary telo kapoaka' = three cups of rice; 'omby roa' = two zebu.
Prices are in ariary (Ar). People often still speak in the old francs — remember 5 francs = 1 ariary when a price sounds five times too big.
Age: 'Firy taona ianao?' — answer right-to-left: 72 = 'roa ambin'ny fitopolo taona aho.'

themes.title: Colours — Ny Loko

words.note: 'Inona ny lokon'ity akanjo ity?' = What colour is this garment?
'Manga ny lanitra' = the sky is blue.
antitra = old/ripe — 'old' blue is dark blue.
tanora = young — 'young' blue is light blue. Colours age: a lovely pattern to remember.
Associated with sovereignty and ceremonies.
Doubling softens a colour: red-red = reddish.
mavo + kely = 'little yellow' = pink.
'Maitsomaitso' = greenish. Note: Tsimihety says 'mahitsy' — but official 'mahitsy' means straight/upright!
'Fotsifotsy' = whitish. White is the mourning colour in much of Madagascar.
Lit. 'orange-fruit coloured' (volo = colour, voasary = orange). Bako writes it 'volomboasary'.
Lit. 'chocolate coloured' (tsokolà = chocolate). Bako: volon-tsokolà.
Lit. 'ash coloured' (davenona = ash/embers).
Lit. 'earth coloured' (tany = soil). Bako: 'Volontany' with Tsimihety 'sokosokolа'.
Parasy is the traditional imported purple-red dye. Bako: 'Volomparasy'.
A compliment for a fine lamba! 'Tsara marevaka ity lamba ity!'
'Miloko samihafa' = multicoloured (of different colours).

culture_notes: Adjectives come AFTER the noun and their order matters less than in English: 'akanjo manga' = a blue garment.
To ask: 'Inona ny lokon'ny ...?' (What colour is the ...?) or 'Inona ny loko tianao?' (What is your favourite colour?) — both from Bako's lesson 6.
Dark-coloured clothes are worn in mourning; bright ones for celebrations (Bako lesson 6).

themes.title: Time & Calendar — Ny Fotoana

words.note: Also 'watch/clock' in the compound famantarandro (off) — Tsimihety uses 'montre'.
Used for DURATIONS, not for telling the time (Bako theme 10).
Also duration only.
Tsimihety: 'Amin'ny firy andro?'
'Fotoan-gasy' ('Malagasy time') — the friendly joke that appointments are flexible.
'Ny andro' doubles as the weather word: 'Manao ahoana ny andro?' = How is the weather?
Note the official spelling 'omaly', though many write 'omaly'.
The everyday word for tomorrow; pairs with omaly (yesterday) and androany (today).
Heard alongside rahampitso in Mandritsara.
Bako's time-of-day table: maraina covers roughly 1–10 am.
'Amin'ny 12 atoandro' = at noon = mitataovovonana.
Bako also writes 'folakandro'.
'Amin'ny 3 folakandro' = at 3 pm.
ALSO means 10,000 in counting — context decides!
Lit. 'half of the night'. Bako's clock table: 00:00.
Lit. 'the sun sits on the ridge of the roof' — a beautiful image.
Lit. 'sun breaks'. Bako's clock table.
Lit. 'the sun dies'.
The weekday names come from traditional cosmology (see culture notes).
'Zoma' also simply means 'week' in some compounds — but the day is Zoma.
From Arabic 'al-had' — the day of the week with an Arabic-name origin.
heri- + andro = 'a span of days'.
The month IS the moon — traditional months follow lunar observation.
Also 'age': 'Firy taona ianao?'
Also a girls' name!
Months simply pair the number with volana for ordinal counting (volana voalohany = January).
The 'thunder-time' of the old year. Opposite: ririnina.
Lit. 'the head of the year'.
Bako: 'equivalent to autumn'.
Lit. 'time of bareness' — grass dries and withers.
Handy for discussing seasons: Madagascar's seasons are the reverse of America's!

construction_rules: Clock time: use numbers 1–12 plus a time-of-day word. 'Amin'ny telo maraina' = at 3 am; 'Amin'ny telo tolakandro' = at 3 pm; 'Amin'ny enina hariva' = at 6 pm. (Bako theme 10.)
'Minitra' and 'segondra' are for durations only ('Nandeha adin-roa izy' = he travelled 2 hours) — not for saying 'it's 3:05'.
Appointments: 'Hihaona amin'ny Zoma amin'ny efatra isika' = We'll meet Friday at four (curriculum Week 8).

Many Malagasy, mostly farmers, also read time from life events: 'maneno akoho' (rooster crows ≈ 3 am), 'vaky masoandro' (sunrise = 6 am), 'mody omby' (zebus come home ≈ 5 pm) — from Bako's clock table.
Past & future with days: 'omaly' (yesterday) and 'rahampitso' (tomorrow) combine with the tense marker on the verb: 'Inona no nataonao omaly?' = What did you do yesterday? (curriculum Week 9).

themes.title: Weather & Nature — Ny Toetr'andro sy ny Zavaboary

words.note: 'Manao ahoana ny andro?' / 'Manakory ny andro?' = How is the weather?
'Ny andro sy ny toetr'andro' = Bako's weather lesson title.
Lit.'eye of the day'. Position of the sun tells morning from afternoon.
'Mandrahona ny andro' = it's cloudy.
'Avy ny orana' / 'latsaka ny orana' = it's raining.
'Mandrivotra ny andro' = it's windy.
'Manga ny lanitra' = the sky is blue.
'Manjavona ny andro' = it's foggy.
'Mitselatra' = there is lightning.
'Mikotroka' = it thunders; 'kotroka' = thunder/the roar of falling water.
'Mafana ny andro' = it's hot (official); Tsimihety: 'mahamay ny andro'.
Bako: 'Mafana ny andro (off) / mahamay ny andro (tsm)'.
'Mangatsiaka ny andro' = it's cold.
Bako: 'Mangatsiaka (off) / manintsy (tsm)'.
The four Malagasy seasons pair hot/cold with humid/dry.
'Maina ny andro' = the weather is dry.
Bako: 'Avy ny orana - latsaka ny orana' = it's raining.
For a weather forecast, 'good weather' means sunny and without rain.
Farmers may not agree — rain at planting time is good news!
Many local names exist; fahavaratra is the big rainy season (roughly Oct-Mar).
Malagasy traditional astrology (mpanandro) reads the day by the kintana.
Same word as month — the moon marks the months.
'Lemaka tany'... 'tany' also appears in maladroit ways — best learned as-is.
Madagascar's trees include the baobab (renala) and the ravinala (traveler's tree).
Lit. 'mother of the forest'; the giant baobabs of the southwest.
The national symbol; its leaf-stems hold drinking water for travelers.
Also 'vony'.
Also 'a sheet of something' (paper etc.).
Used for traditional roofs: 'tafo bozaka'.
Madagascar's eastern rainforest is 'ala mando' (humid forest); the dry spiny forest of the south is very different.
Fishing, washing, and transport all happen on the ony.
Also means 'water hole, inlet'.
Lit. 'salt water' (rano + masina).
The beautiful white-sand beaches of Nosy Be...
Madagascar's highest ridges: the Tsaratanana massif.
From tendrona = tip.

themes.title: Animals — Ny Biby

words.note: 'Biby mampinono' = mammal; 'biby manatody' = egg-laying animal.
Lit. 'little animal'.
'Voronkely' = small bird; 'vorona' covers all birds.
Madagascar's most famous endemic family — over 100 species.
Cat-like predator related to mongooses; hunts lemurs at night.
Lit. 'master of the forest' — 'kandrondro' in Tsimihety.
The task brief's 'camaleinty' maps to the dwarf chameleon of Madagascar - official Malagasy: kankafotra; general word: tanalahy.
Also 'mamba' — an old Bantu loanword. Both are in malagasyword.org.
Careful: 'mamba' in official Malagasy can also mean a python.
Lit. 'long animal'. Madagascar has NO venomous land snakes — a reassuring fact!
The endemic radiated tortoise is 'sokabe'.
The radiated tortoise - sadly nearly extinct in the wild due to poaching.
'Maneno sahona' = the frogs croak (= 2 am, from Bako's clock table!).
The wealth, savings, and splendor of the household; 'omby lahy' = bull.
From 'zebu' via French; 'omby' is the everyday word.
Rural pigs roam freely; henakisoa = pork.
Guardian and companion; usually lives outdoors.
Mousers in the rice stores.
Also the clock: 'maneno akoho tokana' = the rooster crows once (3 am).
Number-first counting: akoho lahy = male chicken.
Lit. 'blue-peacock bird'; 'kolokoloko' in Tsimihety.
Also 'boriky'.
Mangrove crabs are a coastal delicacy.
Lit. 'mother of the honey' — honey (tantely) comes from her.
Traditionally eaten toasted! 'Mendry' in Tsimihety.
One real health concern on the east coast — pack the lay (mosquito net)!
There are no ants in the world quite like Madagascar's... watch the little ones.
Distinct from lolo (butterfly) in some regions.
White birds that follow the zebus in the fields.
Symbol of peace; 'pizina' in Tsimihety.
A scavenging hawk seen circling villages.
The small red sparrow-like bird of the highlands.
Its call marks the arrival of the rainy season in many regions.
The friendly house gecko that eats mosquitoes.
Madagascar has many endemic tenrecs — hedgehog-like insect eaters.
The lemur that 'dances' sideways on the ground.
The largest living lemur; its song carries kilometers in the eastern rainforest.
Humpbacks calve around Sainte-Marie every July–September.
Forest pig, hunted traditionally.
The bright green day geckos (Phelsuma) - emblematic of Madagascar.

culture_notes: Female = vavy, male = lahy, young = zanaka or kely added to the animal's name: akoho lahy = rooster, akoho vavy = hen, akoho zanaka = chick (Bako theme 9).
Zebu carry deep cultural meaning: dowry, sacrifice, funerals, savings, and status. Among some ethnic groups a boy becomes a man after acquiring his first zebu.
Madagascar has no venomous animals — a comforting fact for a nervous traveler (Bako theme 9).
Seeing certain birds (crow, owl) carries superstitious meaning for many Malagasy (Bako theme 9).

themes.title: Body & Health — Ny Vatan'ny Olona sy Ny Aretina

words.note: Also 'colour' in compounds (volom-boasary = orange).
'Aiza ny maso?' = Where are the eyes? — TPR drill from Bako 7a.
Toothache: 'marary nify'.
Also 'language' in the sense of tongue (fiteny = speech/language).
Sore throat: 'marary tenda'.
Chest pain: 'marary tratra'.
Possessive: kiboko = my stomach/belly.
Note the accent: tànana (hand) is different from tanana (town)!
Lit. 'branch of the hand'.
Possessive: tongotro = my foot.
Lit. 'branch of the foot'.
Verified on malagasyword.org.
Verified on malagasyword.org; also 'anything with a bend in it'.
From Bako theme 7a.
'Mafana hoditra izy' = he has a fever (hot skin).
A sensitive word: blood is fady (taboo) in some village contexts - handled indirectly in polite talk.
'Mahasalama ve ianao?' = Are you well?
One word, four uses — Bako theme 7b: 'ny marary' (the patient), 'marary' (painful).
'Mila dokotera aho!' = I need a doctor!
'Aiza ny hopitaly azafady?' = Where is the hospital, please?
Fromody (root) + fan- (instrument): 'that which cures'. Traditional medicine is widely trusted.
Verified on malagasyword.org; also 'famoaham-panafody'.
The single most important emergency word — from the curriculum Week 10 roleplay.
Curriculum Week 10 emergency phrase.
Lit.'caught by the cold'; Tsimihety: 'azon-tsery'.
Tazo can also mean malaria fever (tazo moka = malaria).
'Mosquito fever' (tazo moka) — if fever persists after travel to the coast, insist on a malaria test.
'Marary + body part' = I have pain in ... (Bako theme 7b pattern).
An-doha = on-the-head (liaison n).
'Mikohaka hatramin'ny Talata aho' = I've been coughing since Tuesday.
'Fanina aho' = I feel dizzy (Bako theme 7b).

words.en: There is no pain / nobody is sick.
words.note: Bako theme 7b: a reassuring phrase for the doctor's questions.

words.en: I'm not sick / it doesn't hurt.
words.note: Key answer to the doctor's 'Marary ve?'
Standard doctor's question (Bako theme 7b).

words.en: What is the problem? / what hurts?
words.note: The doctor asks this, literally 'what is the sick one?'
Peace Corps Lesson 6: 'Aiza ny kabone?' = Where is the toilet?
Loanword from French 'douche' (via ladosy).
Peace Corps Lesson 6 feeling.
'Te hatory aho' = I want to sleep.

words.en: to lie down, to go to bed
words.note: 'Mandeha mandry aho' = I'm going to bed (Bako theme 14).
Bako's clock: 'mifoha olo-mazoto' = hard-working people wake up (5 am).

words.en: Are you sick? / does it hurt?
words.note: Simple and essential check-in question.
'Misitranina ny marary.' = The patient is recovering. Past: nisitranina.

culture_notes: Medical infrastructure is limited outside cities; rural Malagasy rely heavily on traditional herbal medicine whose recipes pass down orally (Bako theme 7b).
The possessive suffix attaches to body parts: lohako = my head, tanako = my hand, kiboko = my stomach, tongotro = my foot (curriculum Week 10).
Many villages observe fady (taboos) around certain sicknesses, foods, or places — always ask before overriding a local custom.
Practical elderly-traveler tip: carry written Malagasy emergency sentences ('Vonjeo aho!', 'Mila dokotera aho!', 'Aiza ny hopitaly?') along with your insurance details.

words.note: 'Mihinana vary aho' = I eat rice. Also 'izaho' in formal/written Malagasy.
One word for he AND she — no grammatical gender in Malagasy.
'Isika' and 'izahay' are BOTH 'we', but isika includes the person you're talking to — a fun distinction for an English speaker!
'Izahay' excludes the person you're talking to.

Tsimihety: 'zareo'.
'Iza ianao?' = who are you?; 'Iza no anaranao?' = what is your name?
'Inona no vaovao?' = What's new?

Past nividy, future hividy.

'Faly mandray anao' = happy to welcome you (Bako intro 3).

Also = poor/humble in social contexts.

Goes BEFORE the verb/adjective: 'tsy mihinana' = doesn't eat. First grammar of Week 4.

'___ no anarako' = my name is ___ (lit. 'it is ___ that is my name').
Added at the end of a sentence.

THE humble reply to 'Miteny malagasy ve ianao?' — worth memorizing early!

'Misaotra ianao koa.' = thank you too.
Interchangeable with koa (Bako intro 1b).

grammar_rules: SENTENCE ORDER IS VERB + OBJECT + SUBJECT: 'Mihinana vary aho' literally = 'Eats rice I' = I eat rice. This is the single biggest habit-change for an English speaker (curriculum Week 4).
There is NO verb 'to be': pronouns and adjectives alone carry it — 'Mangatsiaka izy' = she/he/it is cold; 'aho' means both 'I' and 'I am'.
TENSE = FIRST LETTER ONLY: m- (present) → n- (past) → h- (future): mihinana → nihinana → hihinana. Only that first consonant changes (curriculum Week 9).
NEGATION with 'tsy' before the verb: 'Tsy mihinana vary aho' = I don't eat rice; 'Tsy faly izy' = she is not happy.
'Misy/Tsisy' = there is/there isn't: 'Misy atody ve?' = are there eggs? 'Tsisy madinika' = there's no change.
Adjectives STATE the quality directly: 'Mafana ny andro' = the weather is hot; no linking verb needed.
Two 'we's: isika (inclusive, includes the listener) vs izahay (exclusive, leaves the listener out) — one of the most charming features of Malagasy conversation (curriculum Week 2).
